reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it demonstrates ordinary Facebook app functions, including navigating the news feed and menu, uploading photos, checking in, and writing a status post. The speaker is identified as a technology presenter, and the described content concerns social use and desktop-like functionality rather than soliciting money, private credentials, or an off-platform benefit.

citations.quote: I'm going to show you how to use Facebook on a mobile device.
The button on the far right is going to allow you to chat with friends that are online.
you can set your interest, your settings, the app settings, set your favorites, set your privacy settings.
The reason you'd want Facebook on your mobile device is so that you have the same functionality a Facebook has on a desktop except it's while you're on the go.

opening.argument: The video pairs a viewer action with access to the promoted material: it presents a subscription URL and tells viewers that using Facebook on mobile will likely require downloading a dedicated application. That combination can be read as steering viewers into an external subscription or installation flow rather than merely explaining a feature. The presentation does not establish what the subscription delivers, why the application is required, or what permissions the viewer may be granting. Those omissions make the action pathway materially unclear and consistent with a low-barrier acquisition pitch.

citations.quote: Subscribe Now: http://www.youtube.com/subscription_center?add_user=ehowtech
Using Facebook on a mobile device will likely require you to download a dedicated application.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the material an ordinary tutorial does not resolve the solicitation issue. The stated purpose is to get viewers to subscribe, while the practical instruction directs them toward downloading an application. The defense describes functions shown in the clip but does not explain what the subscription provides or why viewers should trust the installation pathway.

citations.quote: Subscribe Now: http://www.youtube.com/subscription_center?add_user=ehowtech
The reason you will want your Facebook app on your device is so that you can connect with your friends and have the same functionality as your desktop.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The cited material shows only a channel-subscription prompt and routine app-use guidance. It does not promise a reward, payment, asset, or withdrawal in exchange for subscribing or installing anything. The application is described as a way to use Facebook, not as a claim or verification flow.

citations.quote: Using Facebook on a mobile device will likely require you to download a dedicated application.
The reason you'd want Facebook on your mobile device is so that you have the same functionality a Facebook has on a desktop except it's while you're on the go.

opening.argument: Several acquisition signals appear together: an explicit subscription URL, advice to install an application, and an in-app menu visibly containing “Offers.” The clip also emphasizes broad access to settings, privacy controls, messaging, photos, and check-ins, while leaving the boundaries of the installation and subscription process unexplained. A careful reviewer should treat that combination as a potentially deceptive low-barrier acquisition funnel, especially because the viewer is encouraged to act before receiving a clear account of what is being obtained or authorized.

citations.quote: Subscribe Now: http://www.youtube.com/subscription_center?add_user=ehowtech
Using Facebook on a mobile device will likely require you to download a dedicated application.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense isolates benign interface functions, but that does not eliminate the visible acquisition cues. The menu includes “Offers,” and the surrounding material directs viewers to subscribe and install an app. The absence of an explicit monetary claim is not proof that the acquisition pathway is harmless or adequately disclosed.

citations.quote: Subscribe Now: http://www.youtube.com/subscription_center?add_user=ehowtech

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The visual menu's “Offers” label does not show a reward, payment, or claim process, and the supplied text never links it to viewer action. The subscription URL is a channel-follow prompt, while the installation statement concerns accessing Facebook. No cited evidence establishes an unusually easy benefit or an asset to acquire.

citations.quote: Using Facebook on a mobile device will likely require you to download a dedicated application.

opening.argument: Although framed as technology education, the presentation functions as promotion: it identifies an expert, repeatedly explains why viewers should use the mobile application, and places a “Subscribe Now” URL alongside the instructional material. The practical effect is to steer viewers toward adoption and continued engagement without presenting limitations, costs, or the consequences of installation. The educational framing therefore should not by itself defeat a scam classification when the content also operates as a low-friction acquisition pitch.

citations.quote: How to Use Facebook on a Mobile Device : Tech Support
Subscribe Now: http://www.youtube.com/subscription_center?add_user=ehowtech
Use Facebook on a mobile device with help from a technology strategist and cloud expert for small to medium businesses in this free video clip.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense treats the speaker's stated role and the described interface as dispositive, but promotional content can use an expert-led instructional format. Here, the educational framing sits next to a direct subscription prompt and repeated encouragement to use the application. That combination supports reading the clip as steering participation, not merely reporting neutral facts.

citations.quote: Subscribe Now: http://www.youtube.com/subscription_center?add_user=ehowtech
The reason you'd want Facebook on your mobile device is so that you have the same functionality a Facebook has on a desktop except it's while you're on the go.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The cited role and subscription prompt do not turn an instructional video into a scam. The material describes ordinary Facebook functions and desktop-like mobile access, but nowhere promises money, rewards, assets, or a benefit obtained by taking an action. Promotion of a free technology tutorial is not evidence of the required reward-action relationship.
